claim_checks.claim: `private` and `protected` are enforced only during type checking. Runtime lookups, and bracket notation even during type checking, still reach the member: it is "soft private".
claim_checks.page_says: private and protected are only enforced during type checking. ... private also allows access using bracket notation during type checking. [probe-01: tsc 5.9.3 exit 0]
claim_checks.note: Type-check-only enforcement and runtime lookup are entailed by [^1]. The handbook gives the bracket-notation escape hatch and the 'soft private' label for private only. The protected part rests on probe-01 alone, a valid probe (tsc would exit non-zero with TS2445), but it shows only TypeScript 5.9.3, and the claim states it as a general rule with no version. That widens the scope: WARN.

claim_checks.claim: `#` fields stay private after compilation and have no bracket-notation escape hatch: they are "hard private".
claim_checks.page_says: JavaScript’s private fields (#) remain private after compilation and do not provide the previously mentioned escape hatches like bracket notation access, making them hard private.

claim_checks.claim: When compiling to ES2021 or lower, TypeScript replaces `#` with `WeakMap`s. The handbook notes that these runtime privacy checks will degrade performance.
claim_checks.page_says: When compiling to ES2021 or less, TypeScript will use WeakMaps in place of #. ... Note that these added privacy checks during runtime could affect performance.
claim_checks.note: The downlevel part is entailed. The handbook says 'could affect', and the claim raises it to 'will degrade', a must-level modal ('will') over a 'could'. The page also aims the note at hard runtime privacy in general (closures, WeakMaps or private fields), not only downleveled output.

claim_checks.claim: Private elements are not properties. They cannot be enumerated, deleted, proxied, or reached through `Object` methods, and `structuredClone()` copies them like public fields.
claim_checks.page_says: they cannot be proxied, enumerated, deleted, or interacted with using any Object method. ... structuredClone() does not clone private elements [probe-02 stdout: false]
claim_checks.note: The first sentence and the enumerate, delete, proxy and Object-method part are entailed. The structuredClone clause says the opposite of [^2]. probe-02 is valid: it tests `#x in structuredClone(new A())` and could print true. It printed false, so it also refutes the clause. The doc contradicts both of its own cited sources.

claim_checks.claim: Reading a `#` field from an object whose class did not declare it throws a `TypeError`. `#x in obj` checks for it without throwing.
claim_checks.page_says: If you access a private element from an object that doesn't have the element, a TypeError is thrown ... You can use the in operator to check whether an externally defined object possesses a private element.
claim_checks.note: The wording 'whose class did not declare it' copies the engine error text that the page shows ("Cannot read private member #x from an object whose class did not declare it").

claim_checks.claim: V8 9.4 moved class-field initialization, including private fields, onto its inline-cache fast path. Before that it went through slower runtime calls.
claim_checks.page_says: Before v9.7, V8 always used a costly runtime call for class field initializations. With v9.7, when V8 considers the pattern of the initialization to be predictable enough
claim_checks.note: The page gives version v9.7, not 9.4, and the doc's own applies-to also says V8 ≥ 9.7. The claim also drops the condition that the IC is used only when the pattern is predictable enough: the page says V8 otherwise 'falls back to a runtime call to deal with the slow cases'.

claim_checks.claim: A `#` name cannot be a parameter property (row: An injected collaborator (port, clock, logger) | `private readonly x` constructor parameter)
claim_checks.page_says: Allow `#`-private names in parameter property positions ... That this is not possible is a bit surprising
claim_checks.note: The text is grounded, but the citation breaches rank quarantine: [^5] is Rank 6 (an issue tracker) in a role 3 section, which allows ranks 1–4. That is recorded as a KB-15 CRITICAL_FAIL. The cached issue is a 2020 feature request, and the first 30 comments show no resolution.

claim_checks.claim: Private elements cannot be proxied (row: Object wrapped in a `Proxy` | `#` access does not go through the proxy)
claim_checks.page_says: they cannot be proxied, enumerated, deleted, or interacted with using any Object method.
claim_checks.note: The cited cell is entailed. The page does not describe what a `#` access on a proxy does. The 'What happens' cell is context and is not graded.

claim_checks.claim: TypeScript downlevels it (row: Target ES2021 or lower | `#` becomes `WeakMap` lookups)
claim_checks.page_says: When compiling to ES2021 or less, TypeScript will use WeakMaps in place of #.

claim_checks.claim: So code meant to run unbuilt keeps injected collaborators as `readonly #field`s assigned in the constructor (row: Working around it with `--experimental-transform-types` | Runs on Node 24.22 with an `ExperimentalWarning` (re-tested 2026-11-03); the flag is removed in Node 26.0.0)
claim_checks.page_says: v26.0.0 | Removed --experimental-transform-types flag. ... parameter properties [listed under features that require transformation]
claim_checks.note: The removal in 26.0.0, and parameter properties needing transformation, are entailed. The row's 'Runs on Node 24.22 with an ExperimentalWarning' is not on the page. A search for 'ExperimentalWarning' and 'experimental' found only the history lines. It rests on an uncited local re-test, although References says [^4] backs it. No probe covers it.

claim_checks.claim: Node only deletes types (row: Type stripping itself | Stable (stability 2) since Node 24.12.0 and 25.2.0; no warning since 24.3.0; Node ignores tsconfig.json and needs .ts extensions in relative imports)
claim_checks.page_says: Since Node.js is only removing inline types, any TypeScript features that involve replacing TypeScript syntax with new JavaScript syntax will error.
claim_checks.note: The row's context is entailed too: history 'v25.2.0, v24.12.0 | Type stripping is now stable', 'v24.3.0, v22.18.0 | ... no longer emits an experimental warning', 'Node.js ignores tsconfig.json files', and file extensions mandatory in import statements.

claim_checks.claim: In Node 24.22.1, `Object.getOwnPropertyNames()` never lists a `#` field
claim_checks.page_says: probe-03 code: `} catch {}` then `console.log('not listed');` [stdout: not listed]
claim_checks.note: probe-03 cannot fail. It never checks whether a private name appears in `names`: its only test is `names.length > 5`. Its try/catch swallows that error anyway, and it prints 'not listed' unconditionally. The claim is true per [^2] ('interacted with using any Object method'), but the doc does not cite [^2] for it.

conflicts.topic: Performance of runtime privacy: [^1] says the added runtime privacy checks 'could affect performance'; the doc's unmarked Summary, Worked example and Takeaways say native `#` costs the same as public fields (a local measurement on Node 24.22). 'Could' is a hedge, so a measured nil difference on one runtime does not contradict it; no arbitration needed. The doc's own contradictions of its cited sources (C4 structuredClone, C6 V8 version) are not source-versus-source conflicts and are counted under grounding.

violations.evidence: Line 48 ('Where each form fits' table, role 3, allowed ranks 1–4) cites [^5], a github.com issue (Rank 6), for 'A `#` name cannot be a parameter property'.
C3: the claim says the handbook notes runtime privacy checks 'will degrade performance'; [^1] says they 'could affect performance' (modal raised to must level).

C4: the claim says '`structuredClone()` copies them like public fields'; [^2] says 'structuredClone() does not clone private elements', and probe-02 printed false for `#x in structuredClone(new A())`.
C6: the claim says 'V8 9.4'; [^3] says the fix shipped in V8 v9.7 ('Before v9.7, V8 always used a costly runtime call'), and the claim drops the 'predictable enough' condition for the IC fast path.
C12: probe-03 swallows errors (`catch {}`), never checks for a `#` name, and prints 'not listed' unconditionally, so it cannot back 'never lists a `#` field'.

C1: [^1] gives the bracket-notation escape hatch and 'soft private' for `private` only. The `protected` bracket access rests on probe-01 alone (TypeScript 5.9.3) but is stated as a general rule with no version.
C10: 'Runs on Node 24.22 with an `ExperimentalWarning` (re-tested 2026-11-03)' is not in [^4]; it rests on an uncited local re-test with no probe.
[^6] (TC39 class fields proposal) is never cited in the body; its References line says it backs How it works 2, but line 36 cites only [^1].

The measurements carry no ✅ or ⚠️, no probe and no local artifact, and the benchmark code is not shown, yet the doc is status: verified with 'Unverified: 0'. The Summary's 'On a native ES2022+ target, reading and creating `#` fields costs the same as public fields' and the Takeaway 'measured cost is nil' generalize this one unbacked run (Node 24.22, V8 13.6) to every native ES2022+ target.

The role 3 mechanism section holds a prescriptive 'Where each form fits' decision table, which is guidance, not mechanism. Its injected-collaborator row recommends a `private readonly x` constructor parameter without the Node type-stripping condition that ## Edge cases raises.
It says 'Verified: 10 claims (✅)', but the body has 12 ✅ claims (lines 35, 36, 37, 38, 39, 40, 48, 66, 67, 69, 70, 95).
